hops.title: Read the back of a vending-machine bestseller
hops.text: Next time you pass a vending machine, turn the bestsellers over and read the panels: peanut-butter crackers, cheese chips, frosted pastries. Many stack fat and carbohydrate in the same bite. In 2018, DiFeliceantonio and colleagues ran a real-money snack auction inside a brain scanner. For snacks matched on average for calories, liking and familiarity, people bid more for combinations than for snacks mainly rich in fat or in carbohydrate, and signals in reward-related brain regions tracked the bids. A 2021 auction found healthy-weight participants bidding more for combinations than for mostly carbohydrate snacks, and no clear effect of snack category in participants with overweight or obesity.

sources.citation: DiFeliceantonio AG et al. Supra-additive effects of combining fat and carbohydrate on food reward. Cell Metab (2018).
Perszyk EE et al. Fat and carbohydrate interactions and food reward. Nutrients (2021).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student standing by a campus vending machine examining the back of a snack package.
image.caption: Healthy-weight volunteers bid more for fat-plus-carbohydrate snacks than for snacks mainly rich in carbohydrate.

hops.afterHeading: GLP-1: three routes, not one relay
hops.title: The Gila monster venom behind the GLP-1 drugs
hops.text: Active GLP-1 from gut L cells has a blood half-life of one to two minutes, partly because an enzyme clips its front end, and that made it a frustrating drug. Separately, looking for a peptide similar to exendin-3, already known from a related lizard, John Eng's team screened Gila monster venom and found exendin-4. It shares GLP-1's first amino acid and resists that clipping. As immediate-release exenatide, it has a mean terminal half-life of about 2.4 hours and became the first approved GLP-1 receptor agonist; semaglutide came by another route, a stabilized GLP-1. A drug that circulates much longer can act in places gut GLP-1 may never reach.

sources.citation: Friedman JM. The discovery and development of GLP-1 based therapeutics. PNAS (2024).
Muller TD et al. Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1). Mol Metab (2019).
Byetta (exenatide) prescribing information, section 12.3 (mean terminal half-life 2.4 h). FDA (2025).
Eng J et al. Isolation and characterization of exendin-4, an exendin-3 analogue, from Heloderma suspectum venom. J Biol Chem (1992).

hops.title: How oral rehydration works in cholera
hops.text: Cholera can make the intestine lose water and salts faster than the body can replace them. In August 1960, Robert Crane brought a sketch to a Prague meeting: one carrier in intestinal cells moves sodium and glucose together. That carrier is SGLT1, the transporter mice need for the vagal response to intestinal sucrose, and it keeps working while the intestine secretes salts and water. Oral rehydration solution pairs glucose and electrolytes in measured proportions, letting SGLT1 absorb sodium and glucose together as water follows. In 1978 The Lancet called that coupling potentially the century's most important medical advance. Oral rehydration still saves millions of lives a year.

audio.title: Three objects behind gut-brain sensing
audio.transcript:
Three objects, none of them a brain: a glass of sugar-salt water, a strip of apple-tree bark, and a venomous desert lizard. Each one sits behind something in this lesson.

Start with the glass of water. In cholera, the intestine can lose water and salts faster than the body can replace them. In August of nineteen sixty, a physiologist named Robert Crane stood up at a meeting in Prague with a sketch of an idea: one carrier in the cells lining the intestine moves sodium and glucose together, with sodium moving into the cell helping bring glucose along. That carrier is S G L T one, the transporter mice need for the vagal response to sucrose delivered into the intestine. Here is the part that saves lives. The coupling keeps working during cholera, even as the intestine secretes salts and water. Oral rehydration solution pairs glucose and electrolytes in measured proportions, letting S G L T one absorb sodium and glucose together as water follows. In nineteen seventy-eight, The Lancet called the discovery that sodium and glucose transport are coupled potentially the most important medical advance of the century, and oral rehydration still saves millions of lives every year.

Now the bark. In the lesson's table, a compound called phloridzin blocked the vagal response to sucrose delivered into the intestine in a mouse experiment. It comes from an orchard. In eighteen thirty-five, Belgian chemists pulled it out of apple-tree root bark, and it was used to treat fever. Fifty years later, in eighteen eighty-six, a German physician named Josef von Mering gave it to dogs and saw something that must have looked like a mistake: glucose pouring into the urine while blood sugar went down. Much later, physiologists worked out the reason. Phloridzin jams sodium-glucose cotransporters, both the intestinal one and the kidney's. Taken by mouth it broke down in the gut, and blocking the intestinal transporter could cause side effects. It inspired diabetes drugs that target the main glucose transporter in the kidney more selectively. The original apple-bark molecule stayed in the lab as the blocker you saw in the table.

Finally, the lizard. The amount of active G L P one in the blood falls by half in about one to two minutes, partly because an enzyme clips off its front end. That short life made it a frustrating drug. A separate discovery in venom eventually offered a way around it. Looking for a peptide similar to exendin-three, already known from a related lizard, an endocrinologist named John Eng and his team screened Gila monster venom and found a peptide called exendin-four. Exendin-four starts with the same amino acid as G L P one and resists that clipping. Its synthetic version, exenatide, became the first approved G L P one receptor-agonist drug, with a mean terminal half-life of about two point four hours in its immediate-release injection. Semaglutide came by a different route: a stabilized version of G L P one itself, not a lizard peptide. That is worth holding on to when you read the G L P one section of this lesson. These drugs can stay in circulation for hours or days, while active G L P one from the gut is cleared much faster. In rodent studies, some long-acting drugs reach specific brain regions, which still leaves open whether gut G L P one takes that route.
